title: By night, from mosque to mosque
hook: glory to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque (17:1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, patience through Him, the last gift of An-Nahl. Your line was patience is from him. When yours ran low, did you stop and ask? Day four hundred fifty-seven, and a new surah.

Surah seventeen opens with one of the most talked-about nights in Muslim history, and it tells it in a single verse. No buildup, no description of the road. Just a sentence of praise, and inside it, a journey. The surah is named for that night: Al-Isra, the Night Journey. Its other name is Bani Isra'il, the Children of Israel. Many Muslims mark the night every year, often on the twenty-seventh of the month of Rajab, though the date is debated. Today: the verse.

In Pickthall's translation: "Glorified be He Who carried His servant by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship". The verse goes on: whose surroundings We have blessed, so that We might show him some of Our signs. Start with the first word, subhana: glory be, far above any fault. The verse opens with praise of the One who did the carrying, not the one who was carried. And notice what he's called. Not prophet, not messenger. 'Abd: servant. On the greatest night of his life, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is named by the humblest title. Then the two places. The Sacred Mosque is in Mecca, around the Ka'bah. The Farthest Mosque, al-Masjid al-Aqsa, is understood by Muslims as Jerusalem. Masjid literally means a place of prostration, a place where people bow. The hadith collections fill in what the verse leaves out. In Bukhari and Muslim, a white mount called Buraq carries him; in Jerusalem he leads the earlier prophets in prayer; and from there comes the Mi'raj, the ascent through the heavens, where the five daily prayers are given. Scholars have discussed the nature of the journey from early on. Most hold it was in body and spirit; a few early reports describe it as spiritual. Both views have long had defenders. The biographies place it in a hard season, after the Prophet had lost his wife Khadijah and his uncle Abu Talib, when doors in Mecca and Ta'if were closing. So the night comes when the days were darkest. Taken by night: not carried away from trouble, but shown signs in the middle of it.
screen: `SUBHANA: GLORY TO THE ONE WHO CARRIED.` · `'ABD: HIS HUMBLEST TITLE.` · `MECCA TO JERUSALEM, THEN THE ASCENT.` · `THE NIGHT AFTER THE HARDEST YEAR.` · then, large: `BY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Tonight, or now if it's dark, look at the night sky. If you can't get outside, a window is fine, or simply close your eyes and remember the last clear night you saw. Notice how far away the farthest light is. Let yourself feel small under it, not in a bad way. Then think of one dark stretch in your own life, and one thing you only saw because of it. If you pray, you can say subhan Allah, glory to God, once, quietly. The bell holds the time.
By night. The Isra: a servant carried from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, in the dark, to be shown signs. Today's word.
Your line: taken by night. Today, when something feels dark or closed, ask what it might be showing you that the easy days couldn't. Day four hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Many Muslims mark Laylat al-Isra wal-Mi'raj, often on 27 Rajab, with extra prayer, Qur'an recitation and talks retelling the journey; practice varies, and some scholars caution against fixing special rites to the date.

fork.setup: you've lost your wife and your uncle in the same season, and doors are closing around you. what does the night bring, as the tradition tells it?
options: a sign that it's time to give up.
a journey by night, and signs shown to him.
an easy year with no more trouble.
fork.reveal: he is carried by night from Mecca to Jerusalem and shown signs, in the middle of the hardest season, not after it.

original.note: Arabic: He carried His servant by night (17:1). Isra, the night journey, comes from this verb.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a miraculous trip.
what it means: the verse praises God, calls Muhammad a servant, and sets the journey from Mecca to Jerusalem in one sentence.
what a scholar hears: asra already means to travel by night, yet the verse adds laylan, by night; commentators say it stresses a part of a single night.
